core: Working definition of global business: buying, selling, and operating across national borders (OpenStax Introduction to Business chapter 3: exports/imports for buying and selling; multinational corporations for operating).
Why companies go global: new markets, lower costs, resource access — each named with one line.
Trade basics: imports, exports, and the balance of trade (surplus vs deficit), each named simply; economics-and-business referenced only.
The global environment: currency (exchange rates), culture, and regulations — each named as a factor to navigate, with an original example.
Globalization: the growing interconnection of economies — stated factually.
Multinational companies: businesses that operate in many countries — named generally.
Honest framing: going global multiplies opportunity and complexity — the reality check.
supporting: Exporting as the least complicated, least risky entry mode (OpenStax 3.6).
Current U.S. trade-deficit figure from BEA (June 2026) as a concrete anchor for the trade-deficit concept.
Trade's benefits (lower prices, larger markets, innovation) and costs (job displacement) both real — stated without advocacy (OpenStax 3.2, Investopedia).
outOfScope: Comparative advantage, trade theory, and why-nations-trade economics — owned by economics-and-business.
PEST-style environment frameworks — owned by business-environment.
Logistics, sourcing, and supply-chain depth — owned by supply-chain-basics.
Tariff policy debates and trade-war positions — deliberately excluded; factual framing only.
Country-specific stereotypes and named-company deep dives.

claims.claim: Global business is buying, selling, and operating across national borders: exports and imports are the buying and selling activities, and multinational corporations are the operating activity.
Exports are goods and services made in one country and sold to others; imports are goods and services bought from other countries.

The balance of trade is the difference between the value of a country's exports and the value of its imports during a specific period; exporting more than importing is a trade surplus, and importing more than exporting is a trade deficit.

The United States currently imports more than it exports: in June 2026, U.S. exports of goods and services were $314.7 billion and imports $388.0 billion, a monthly goods-and-services deficit of $73.3 billion.
Companies go global to earn additional profits, to escape saturated domestic markets, and to capture potential cost savings.
Businesses go global to reach new consumer markets, to lower manufacturing and material costs, and to source materials internationally.
Nations cannot produce everything at home — resources such as cobalt and coffee are only available in certain places — so businesses cross borders to access inputs their home country lacks.
The exchange rate is the price of one country's currency in terms of another country's currency, and it changes what goods cost across borders.

Culture — the common set of values in a society, including language and customs — has a large effect on customer preferences, and businesses must take political and cultural differences into account to succeed abroad.
Governments create barriers to trade and other conditions — tariffs, quotas, and regulation — that companies must navigate when operating in foreign markets.
Globalization is the increasing interconnectedness of countries through trade, investment, technology, and the movement of goods and services.

Multinational corporations move resources, goods, services, and skills across national boundaries without regard to the country in which their headquarters are located, and they are heavily engaged in international trade.
Exporting is usually the least complicated and least risky way for a company to enter the global market.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether globalization and free trade are good or bad overall.
positions: Benefits: productivity grows faster with specialization, living standards can rise, competition keeps prices down, and open economies spur innovation (OpenStax 3.2).
Costs: millions of workers face job displacement from imports and production moving abroad, and many people fear the effects of trade (OpenStax 3.2).
Investopedia's Globalization article takes a neutral 'it depends' stance, weighing both sides.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both benefits and costs factually without taking an advocacy position: going global multiplies opportunity and complexity, and reasonable people weigh them differently.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a trade deficit is 'bad' for a country.
positions: OpenStax uses the traditional labels 'favorable' (surplus) and 'unfavorable' (deficit).
Economists note deficits can also reflect strong consumer demand and can be read in context; the label itself carries no verdict.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines the terms and reports the current U.S. figure from BEA without judgment, and a common-mistake entry notes that a deficit is not automatically bad.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 3.1: Global Trade in the United States
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: exports are goods and services made in one country and sold to others; imports are goods and services bought from other countries; the balance of trade as the difference between export and import value with trade surplus (exports exceed imports) and trade deficit (imports exceed exports) as the two directions; the exchange rate as the price of one country's currency in terms of another's, with appreciation/depreciation effects on prices; the United States as the largest importer and second largest exporter; and the 'global vision' framing of international business. Section used as reference per OpenStax's no-LLM-ingestion notice; all facts restated in original prose with attribution; no wording reproduced.
